Suggestion: Sliding Window Function
Using `np.lib.stride_tricks.as_stride` one can very efficiently create a sliding window that segments an array as a preprocessing step for vectorized applications. For example a moving average of a window length `3`, stepsize `1`:

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
a_strided = numpy.lib.stride_tricks.as_strided(
    a, shape=(8, 3), strides=(8, 8)
)
print numpy.mean(a_strided, axis=1)
```

This is very performant but very hard to do, as the `shape` and `strides` parameters are very hard to understand.

I suggest the implementation of a "simple `sliding_window` function" that does the job of figuring out those two parameters for you.

[The implementation I have been using for years](https://gist.github.com/nils-werner/9d321441006b112a4b116a8387c2280c) allows the above to be replaced by

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
a_strided = sliding_window(a, size=3, stepsize=1)
print numpy.mean(a_strided, axis=1)
```

@teoliphant [also has an implementation](https://gist.github.com/teoliphant/96eb779a16bd038e374f2703da62f06d) that would change the above to

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
a_strided = array_for_sliding_window(a, 3)
print numpy.mean(a_strided, axis=1)
```

both making it much more readable.

Seeing it is a common usecase in vectorized computing I suggest we put a similar function into NumPy itself.

Regarding to which implementation to follow, they are both assume different things but allow you to do the same thing eventually:

`sliding_window`
- slides over one axis only
- allows setting windowsize and stepsize
- returns array with dimension n+1
- sliding over several axes requires two calls (which come for free as there is no memory reordered)
- has a superfluous `copy` parameter that can be removed and replaced by appending `.copy()` after the call

`array_for_sliding_window`
- slides over all axes simultaneously, window lengths are given as `tuple` parameter
- Assumes a stepsize one in all directions
- returns array with dimension n*2
- stepsize not equal to one requires slicing of output data (unsure if this implies copying data)
- Disabling sliding over `axis[n]` requires you set argument `wshape[n] = 1` or `wshape[n] = a.shape[n]`

This means for flexible `stepsize` the following are equivalent (with some minor bug in `sliding_window` there):

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
print sliding_window(a, size=3, stepsize=2)

a = numpy.arange(10)
print array_for_sliding_window(a, 3)[::2, :] # Stepsize 2 by dropping every 2nd row
```

for sliding over one `axis` the following are equivalent (with some transposing and squeezing):

```
a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print sliding_window(a, size=3, axis=1)

a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print array_for_sliding_window(a, (1, 3))
```

and for sliding over two `axis` the following are equivalent:

```
a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print sliding_window(sliding_window(a, size=3, axis=0), size=2, axis=1)

a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print array_for_sliding_window(a, (3, 2))
```

This issue is about sparking discussion about
- Do we need such a function?
- Which features are required?
- Which interface should we persue?

After discussion I am willing to draft up a pull request with an implementation we agreed on.

+def _sliding_window_view_dispatcher(x, window_shape, axis=None, *,
+                                    subok=None, writeable=None):

+@array_function_dispatch(_sliding_window_view_dispatcher, module='numpy')
+def sliding_window_view(x, window_shape, axis=None, *,
+                        subok=False, writeable=False):
+    """
+    Create a sliding window view into the array with the given window shape.
+
+    Also known as rolling or moving window, the window slides across all
+    dimensions of the array and extracts subsets of the array at all window
+    positions.
+    
+    .. versionadded:: 1.20.0
+
+    Parameters
+    ----------
+    x : array_like
+        Array to create the sliding window view from.
+    window_shape : int or tuple of int
+        Size of window over each axis that takes part in the sliding window.
+        If `axis` is not present, must have same length as the number of input
+        array dimensions. Single integers `i` are treated as if they were the
+        tuple `(i,)`.
+    axis : int or tuple of int, optional
+        Axis or axes along which the sliding window is applied.
+        By default, the sliding window is applied to all axes and
+        `window_shape[i]` will refer to axis `i` of `x`.
+        If `axis` is given as a `tuple of int`, `window_shape[i]` will refer to
+        the axis `axis[i]` of `x`.
+        Single integers `i` are treated as if they were the tuple `(i,)`.
+    subok : bool, optional
+        If True, sub-classes will be passed-through, otherwise the returned
+        array will be forced to be a base-class array (default).
+    writeable : bool, optional
+        When true, allow writing to the returned view. The default is false,
+        as this should be used with caution: the returned view contains the
+        same memory location multiple times, so writing to one location will
+        cause others to change.
+
+    Returns
+    -------
+    view : ndarray
+        Sliding window view of the array. The sliding window dimensions are
+        inserted at the end, and the original dimensions are trimmed as
+        required by the size of the sliding window.
+        That is, ``view.shape = x_shape_trimmed + window_shape``, where
+        ``x_shape_trimmed`` is ``x.shape`` with every entry reduced by one less
+        than the corresponding window size.
+
+    See Also
+    --------
+    lib.stride_tricks.as_strided: A lower-level and less safe routine for
+        creating arbitrary views from custom shape and strides.
+    broadcast_to: broadcast an array to a given shape.
+
+    Notes
+    -----
+    For many applications using a sliding window view can be convenient, but
+    potentially very slow. Often specialized solutions exist, for example:
+
+    - `scipy.signal.fftconvolve`
+
+    - filtering functions in `scipy.ndimage`
+
+    - moving window functions provided by
+      `bottleneck <https://github.com/pydata/bottleneck>`_.
+
+    As a rough estimate, a sliding window approach with an input size of `N`
+    and a window size of `W` will scale as `O(N*W)` where frequently a special
+    algorithm can achieve `O(N)`. That means that the sliding window variant
+    for a window size of 100 can be a 100 times slower than a more specialized
+    version.
+
+    Nevertheless, for small window sizes, when no custom algorithm exists, or
+    as a prototyping and developing tool, this function can be a good solution.
+
+    Examples
+    --------
+    >>> x = np.arange(6)
+    >>> x.shape
+    (6,)
+    >>> v = np.sliding_window_view(x, 3)
+    >>> v.shape
+    (4, 3)
+    >>> v
+    array([[0, 1, 2],
+           [1, 2, 3],
+           [2, 3, 4],
+           [3, 4, 5]])
+
+    This also works in more dimensions, e.g.
+
+    >>> i, j = np.ogrid[:3, :4]
+    >>> x = 10*i + j
+    >>> x.shape
+    (3, 4)
+    >>> x
+    array([[ 0,  1,  2,  3],
+           [10, 11, 12, 13],
+           [20, 21, 22, 23]])
+    >>> shape = (2,2)
+    >>> v = np.sliding_window_view(x, shape)
+    >>> v.shape
+    (2, 3, 2, 2)
+    >>> v
+    array([[[[ 0,  1],
+             [10, 11]],
+            [[ 1,  2],
+             [11, 12]],
+            [[ 2,  3],
+             [12, 13]]],
+           [[[10, 11],
+             [20, 21]],
+            [[11, 12],
+             [21, 22]],
+            [[12, 13],
+             [22, 23]]]])
+
+    The axis can be specified explicitly:
+
+    >>> v = np.sliding_window_view(x, 3, 0)
+    >>> v.shape
+    (1, 4, 3)
+    >>> v
+    array([[[ 0, 10, 20],
+            [ 1, 11, 21],
+            [ 2, 12, 22],
+            [ 3, 13, 23]]])
+
+    The same axis can be used several times. In that case, every use reduces
+    the corresponding original dimension:
+
+    >>> v = np.sliding_window_view(x, (2, 3), (1, 1))
+    >>> v.shape
+    (3, 1, 2, 3)
+    >>> v
+    array([[[[ 0,  1,  2],
+             [ 1,  2,  3]]],
+           [[[10, 11, 12],
+             [11, 12, 13]]],
+           [[[20, 21, 22],
+             [21, 22, 23]]]])
+
+    Combining with stepped slicing (`::step`), this can be used to take sliding
+    views which skip elements:
+
+    >>> x = np.arange(7)
+    >>> np.sliding_window_view(x, 5)[:, ::2]
+    array([[0, 2, 4],
+           [1, 3, 5],
+           [2, 4, 6]])
+
+    or views which move by multiple elements
+
+    >>> x = np.arange(7)
+    >>> np.sliding_window_view(x, 3)[::2, :]
+    array([[0, 1, 2],
+           [2, 3, 4],
+           [4, 5, 6]])
+
+    A common application of `sliding_window_view` is the calculation of running
+    statistics. The simplest example is the
+    `moving average <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moving_average>`_:
+
+    >>> x = np.arange(6)
+    >>> x.shape
+    (6,)
+    >>> v = np.sliding_window_view(x, 3)
+    >>> v.shape
+    (4, 3)
+    >>> v
+    array([[0, 1, 2],
+           [1, 2, 3],
+           [2, 3, 4],
+           [3, 4, 5]])
+    >>> moving_average = v.mean(axis=-1)
+    >>> moving_average
+    array([1., 2., 3., 4.])
+
+    Note that a sliding window approach is often **not** optimal (see Notes).
+    """
+    window_shape = (tuple(window_shape)
+                    if np.iterable(window_shape)
+                    else (window_shape,))
+    # first convert input to array, possibly keeping subclass
+    x = np.array(x, copy=False, subok=subok)
+
+    window_shape_array = np.array(window_shape)
+    if np.any(window_shape_array < 0):
+        raise ValueError('`window_shape` cannot contain negative values')
+
+    if axis is None:
+        axis = tuple(range(x.ndim))
+        if len(window_shape) != len(axis):
+            raise ValueError(f'Since axis is `None`, must provide '
+                             f'window_shape for all dimensions of `x`; '
+                             f'got {len(window_shape)} window_shape elements '
+                             f'and `x.ndim` is {x.ndim}.')
+    else:
+        axis = normalize_axis_tuple(axis, x.ndim, allow_duplicate=True)
+        if len(window_shape) != len(axis):
+            raise ValueError(f'Must provide matching length window_shape and '
+                             f'axis; got {len(window_shape)} window_shape '
+                             f'elements and {len(axis)} axes elements.')
+
+    out_strides = x.strides + tuple(x.strides[ax] for ax in axis)
+
+    # note: same axis can be windowed repeatedly
+    x_shape_trimmed = list(x.shape)
+    for ax, dim in zip(axis, window_shape):
+        if x_shape_trimmed[ax] < dim:
+            raise ValueError(
+                'window shape cannot be larger than input array shape')
+        x_shape_trimmed[ax] -= dim - 1
+    out_shape = tuple(x_shape_trimmed) + window_shape
+    return as_strided(x, strides=out_strides, shape=out_shape,
+                      subok=subok, writeable=writeable)
+
+
 def _broadcast_to(array, shape, subok, readonly):
     shape = tuple(shape) if np.iterable(shape) else (shape,)
     array = np.array(array, copy=False, subok=subok)

Title: Suggestion: Sliding Window Function

Using `np.lib.stride_tricks.as_stride` one can very efficiently create a sliding window that segments an array as a preprocessing step for vectorized applications. For example a moving average of a window length `3`, stepsize `1`:

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
a_strided = numpy.lib.stride_tricks.as_strided(
    a, shape=(8, 3), strides=(8, 8)
)
print numpy.mean(a_strided, axis=1)
```

This is very performant but very hard to do, as the `shape` and `strides` parameters are very hard to understand.

I suggest the implementation of a "simple `sliding_window` function" that does the job of figuring out those two parameters for you.

[The implementation I have been using for years](https://gist.github.com/nils-werner/9d321441006b112a4b116a8387c2280c) allows the above to be replaced by

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
a_strided = sliding_window(a, size=3, stepsize=1)
print numpy.mean(a_strided, axis=1)
```

@teoliphant [also has an implementation](https://gist.github.com/teoliphant/96eb779a16bd038e374f2703da62f06d) that would change the above to

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
a_strided = array_for_sliding_window(a, 3)
print numpy.mean(a_strided, axis=1)
```

both making it much more readable.

Seeing it is a common usecase in vectorized computing I suggest we put a similar function into NumPy itself.

Regarding to which implementation to follow, they are both assume different things but allow you to do the same thing eventually:

`sliding_window`
- slides over one axis only
- allows setting windowsize and stepsize
- returns array with dimension n+1
- sliding over several axes requires two calls (which come for free as there is no memory reordered)
- has a superfluous `copy` parameter that can be removed and replaced by appending `.copy()` after the call

`array_for_sliding_window`
- slides over all axes simultaneously, window lengths are given as `tuple` parameter
- Assumes a stepsize one in all directions
- returns array with dimension n*2
- stepsize not equal to one requires slicing of output data (unsure if this implies copying data)
- Disabling sliding over `axis[n]` requires you set argument `wshape[n] = 1` or `wshape[n] = a.shape[n]`

This means for flexible `stepsize` the following are equivalent (with some minor bug in `sliding_window` there):

```
a = numpy.arange(10)
print sliding_window(a, size=3, stepsize=2)

a = numpy.arange(10)
print array_for_sliding_window(a, 3)[::2, :] # Stepsize 2 by dropping every 2nd row
```

for sliding over one `axis` the following are equivalent (with some transposing and squeezing):

```
a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print sliding_window(a, size=3, axis=1)

a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print array_for_sliding_window(a, (1, 3))
```

and for sliding over two `axis` the following are equivalent:

```
a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print sliding_window(sliding_window(a, size=3, axis=0), size=2, axis=1)

a = numpy.arange(25).reshape(5, 5)
print array_for_sliding_window(a, (3, 2))
```

This issue is about sparking discussion about
- Do we need such a function?
- Which features are required?
- Which interface should we persue?

After discussion I am willing to draft up a pull request with an implementation we agreed on.
--- END PROBLEM STATEMENT ---

# Search for code content contain keyword `order`, `bill`
search_code_snippets(search_terms=["order", "bill"])

search_code_snippets(search_terms=["MyClass"])

search_code_snippets(line_nums=[10, 15], file_path_or_pattern='src/example.py')

file_path_or_pattern.description: A glob pattern or specific file path used to filter search results to particular files or directories. Defaults to "**/*.py", meaning all Python files are searched by default. If `line_nums` are provided, this must specify a specific file path.

841 |     """Compute true and predicted probabilities for a calibration curve.
842 | 
843 |     The method assumes the inputs come from a binary classifier, and
844 |     discretize the [0, 1] interval into bins.
845 | 
846 |     Calibration curves may also be referred to as reliability diagrams.
847 | 
848 |     Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <calibration>`.

854 |

857 | 
858 |     normalize : bool, default=False
859 |         Whether y_prob needs to be normalized into the [0, 1] interval, i.e.
860 |         is not a proper probability. If True, the smallest value in y_prob
861 |         is linearly mapped onto 0 and the largest one onto 1.
862 | 
863 |     n_bins : int, default=5
864 |         Number of bins to discretize the [0, 1] interval. A bigger number
865 |         requires more data. Bins with no samples (i.e. without
866 |         corresponding values in `y_prob`) will not be returned, thus the
867 |         returned arrays may have less than `n_bins` values.
868 | 
869 |     strategy : {'uniform', 'quantile'}, default='uniform'
870 |         Strategy used to define the widths of the bins.
871 | 
872 |         uniform
873 |             The bins have identical widths.
874 |         quantile
875 |             The bins have the same number of samples and depend on `y_prob`.
876 | 
877 |     Returns
878 |     -------
879 |     prob_true : ndarray of shape (n_bins,) or smaller
880 |         The proportion of samples whose class is the positive class, in each
881 |         bin (fraction of positives).
882 | 
883 |     prob_pred : ndarray of shape (n_bins,) or smaller
884 |         The mean predicted probability in each bin.
885 | 
886 |     References
887 |     ----------
888 |     Alexandru Niculescu-Mizil and Rich Caruana (2005) Predicting Good
889 |     Probabilities With Supervised Learning, in Proceedings of the 22nd
890 |     International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML).
891 |     See section 4 (Qualitative Analysis of Predictions).
892 | 
893 |     Examples
894 |     --------
895 |     >>> import numpy as np
896 |     >>> from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve
897 |     >>> y_true = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1])
898 |     >>> y_pred = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.65, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9,  1.])
899 |     >>> prob_true, prob_pred = calibration_curve(y_true, y_pred, n_bins=3)
900 |     >>> prob_true
901 |     array([0. , 0.5, 1. ])
902 |     >>> prob_pred
903 |     array([0.2  , 0.525, 0.85 ])
904 |     """
905 |     y_true = column_or_1d(y_true)
906 |     y_prob = column_or_1d(y_prob)
907 |     check_consistent_length(y_true, y_prob)
908 | 
909 |     if normalize:  # Normalize predicted values into interval [0, 1]
910 |         y_prob = (y_prob - y_prob.min()) / (y_prob.max() - y_prob.min())
911 |     elif y_prob.min() < 0 or y_prob.max() > 1:
912 |         raise ValueError(
913 |             "y_prob has values outside [0, 1] and normalize is set to False."
914 |         )
915 |

917 |     if len(labels) > 2:
918 |         raise ValueError(
919 |             "Only binary classification is supported. Provided labels %s." % labels
920 |         )
921 |     y_true = label_binarize(y_true, classes=labels)[:, 0]
922 | 
923 |     if strategy == "quantile":  # Determine bin edges by distribution of data
924 |         quantiles = np.linspace(0, 1, n_bins + 1)
925 |         bins = np.percentile(y_prob, quantiles * 100)
926 |         bins[-1] = bins[-1] + 1e-8
927 |     elif strategy == "uniform":
928 |         bins = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0 + 1e-8, n_bins + 1)
929 |     else:
930 |         raise ValueError(
931 |             "Invalid entry to 'strategy' input. Strategy "
932 |             "must be either 'quantile' or 'uniform'."
933 |         )
934 | 
935 |     binids = np.digitize(y_prob, bins) - 1
936 | 
937 |     bin_sums = np.bincount(binids, weights=y_prob, minlength=len(bins))
938 |     bin_true = np.bincount(binids, weights=y_true, minlength=len(bins))
939 |     bin_total = np.bincount(binids, minlength=len(bins))
940 | 
941 |     nonzero = bin_total != 0
942 |     prob_true = bin_true[nonzero] / bin_total[nonzero]
943 |     prob_pred = bin_sums[nonzero] / bin_total[nonzero]
944 |

757 |     T[y > 0] = (prior1 + 1.0) / (prior1 + 2.0)

759 |     T1 = 1.0 - T

763 |         P = expit(-(AB[0] * F + AB[1]))

767 |         else:
768 |             return loss.sum()

774 |         if sample_weight is not None:
775 |             TEP_minus_T1P *= sample_weight
776 |         dA = np.dot(TEP_minus_T1P, F)

722 | def _sigmoid_calibration(predictions, y, sample_weight=None):
723 |     """Probability Calibration with sigmoid method (Platt 2000)
724 | 
725 |     Parameters
726 |     ----------
727 |     predictions : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
728 |         The decision function or predict proba for the samples.
729 | 
730 |     y : ndarray of shape (n_samples,)
731 |         The targets.
732 | 
733 |     sample_weight : array-like of shape (n_samples,), default=None
734 |         Sample weights. If None, then samples are equally weighted.
735 | 
736 |     Returns
737 |     -------
738 |     a : float
739 |         The slope.
740 | 
741 |     b : float
742 |         The intercept.
743 | 
744 |     References
745 |     ----------
746 |     Platt, "Probabilistic Outputs for Support Vector Machines"
747 |     """
748 |     predictions = column_or_1d(predictions)
749 |     y = column_or_1d(y)
750 | 
751 |     F = predictions  # F follows Platt's notations
752 | 
753 |     # Bayesian priors (see Platt end of section 2.2)
754 |     prior0 = float(np.sum(y <= 0))
755 |     prior1 = y.shape[0] - prior0
756 |     T = np.zeros(y.shape)
757 |     T[y > 0] = (prior1 + 1.0) / (prior1 + 2.0)
758 |     T[y <= 0] = 1.0 / (prior0 + 2.0)
759 |     T1 = 1.0 - T
760 | 
761 |     def objective(AB):
762 |         # From Platt (beginning of Section 2.2)
763 |         P = expit(-(AB[0] * F + AB[1]))
764 |         loss = -(xlogy(T, P) + xlogy(T1, 1.0 - P))
765 |         if sample_weight is not None:
766 |             return (sample_weight * loss).sum()
767 |         else:
768 |             return loss.sum()
769 | 
770 |     def grad(AB):
771 |         # gradient of the objective function
772 |         P = expit(-(AB[0] * F + AB[1]))
773 |         TEP_minus_T1P = T - P
774 |         if sample_weight is not None:
775 |             TEP_minus_T1P *= sample_weight
776 |         dA = np.dot(TEP_minus_T1P, F)
777 |         dB = np.sum(TEP_minus_T1P)
778 |         return np.array([dA, dB])
779 | 
780 |     AB0 = np.array([0.0, log((prior0 + 1.0) / (prior1 + 1.0))])
781 |     AB_ = fmin_bfgs(objective, AB0, fprime=grad, disp=False)
782 |     return AB_[0], AB_[1]

Add sparse matrix output to SplineTransformer
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

As B-splines naturally have a sparse structure, I'd like to have the option that `SplineTransformer` returns a sparse matrix instead of always an ndarray.
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import SplineTransformer

X = np.arange(6).reshape(6, 1)
spline = SplineTransformer(degree=2, n_knots=3, sparse=True)
spline.fit_transform(X)
```

### Describe your proposed solution

With scipy >= 1.8 (yet to be released), we can use `design_matrix` from https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/14344.

  96 | class PolynomialFeatures(TransformerMixin, BaseEstimator):
  97 |     """Generate polynomial and interaction features.
  98 | 
  99 |     Generate a new feature matrix consisting of all polynomial combinations
 100 |     of the features with degree less than or equal to the specified degree.
 101 |     For example, if an input sample is two dimensional and of the form
 102 |     [a, b], the degree-2 polynomial features are [1, a, b, a^2, ab, b^2].
 103 | 
 104 |     Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <polynomial_features>`.
 105 | 
 106 |     Parameters
 107 |     ----------
 108 |     degree : int or tuple (min_degree, max_degree), default=2
 109 |         If a single int is given, it specifies the maximal degree of the
 110 |         polynomial features. If a tuple `(min_degree, max_degree)` is passed,
 111 |         then `min_degree` is the minimum and `max_degree` is the maximum
 112 |         polynomial degree of the generated features. Note that `min_degree=0`
 113 |         and `min_degree=1` are equivalent as outputting the degree zero term is
 114 |         determined by `include_bias`.
 115 | 
 116 |     interaction_only : bool, default=False
 117 |         If `True`, only interaction features are produced: features that are
 118 |         products of at most `degree` *distinct* input features, i.e. terms with
 119 |         power of 2 or higher of the same input feature are excluded:
 120 | 
 121 |             - included: `x[0]`, `x[1]`, `x[0] * x[1]`, etc.
 122 |             - excluded: `x[0] ** 2`, `x[0] ** 2 * x[1]`, etc.
 123 | 
 124 |     include_bias : bool, default=True
 125 |         If `True` (default), then include a bias column, the feature in which
 126 |         all polynomial powers are zero (i.e. a column of ones - acts as an
 127 |         intercept term in a linear model).
 128 | 
 129 |     order : {'C', 'F'}, default='C'
 130 |         Order of output array in the dense case. `'F'` order is faster to
 131 |         compute, but may slow down subsequent estimators.
 132 | 
 133 |         .. versionadded:: 0.21
 134 | 
 135 |     Attributes
 136 |     ----------
 137 |     powers_ : ndarray of shape (`n_output_features_`, `n_features_in_`)
 138 |         `powers_[i, j]` is the exponent of the jth input in the ith output.
 139 | 
 140 |     n_features_in_ : int
 141 |         Number of features seen during :term:`fit`.
 142 | 
 143 |         .. versionadded:: 0.24
 144 | 
 145 |     feature_names_in_ : ndarray of shape (`n_features_in_`,)
 146 |         Names of features seen during :term:`fit`. Defined only when `X`
 147 |         has feature names that are all strings.
 148 | 
 149 |         .. versionadded:: 1.0
 150 | 
 151 |     n_output_features_ : int
 152 |         The total number of polynomial output features. The number of output
 153 |         features is computed by iterating over all suitably sized combinations
 154 |         of input features.
 155 | 
 156 |     See Also
 157 |     --------
 158 |     SplineTransformer : Transformer that generates univariate B-spline bases
 159 |         for features.
 160 | 
 161 |     Notes
 162 |     -----
 163 |     Be aware that the number of features in the output array scales
 164 |     polynomially in the number of features of the input array, and
 165 |     exponentially in the degree. High degrees can cause overfitting.
 166 | 
 167 |     See :ref:`examples/linear_model/plot_polynomial_interpolation.py
 168 |     <sphx_glr_auto_examples_linear_model_plot_polynomial_interpolation.py>`
 169 | 
 170 |     Examples
 171 |     --------
 172 |     >>> import numpy as np
 173 |     >>> from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
 174 |     >>> X = np.arange(6).reshape(3, 2)
 175 |     >>> X
 176 |     array([[0, 1],
 177 |            [2, 3],
 178 |            [4, 5]])
 179 |     >>> poly = PolynomialFeatures(2)
 180 |     >>> poly.fit_transform(X)
 181 |     array([[ 1.,  0.,  1.,  0.,  0.,  1.],
 182 |            [ 1.,  2.,  3.,  4.,  6.,  9.],
 183 |            [ 1.,  4.,  5., 16., 20., 25.]])
 184 |     >>> poly = PolynomialFeatures(interaction_only=True)
 185 |     >>> poly.fit_transform(X)
 186 |     array([[ 1.,  0.,  1.,  0.],
 187 |            [ 1.,  2.,  3.,  6.],
 188 |            [ 1.,  4.,  5., 20.]])
 189 |     """
 190 | 
 191 |     _parameter_constraints: dict = {
 192 |         "degree": [Interval(Integral, 0, None, closed="left"), "array-like"],
 193 |         "interaction_only": ["boolean"],
 194 |         "include_bias": ["boolean"],
 195 |         "order": [StrOptions({"C", "F"})],
 196 |     }
 197 | 
 198 |     def __init__(
 199 |         self, degree=2, *, interaction_only=False, include_bias=True, order="C"
 200 |     ):
 201 |         self.degree = degree
 202 |         self.interaction_only = interaction_only
 203 |         self.include_bias = include_bias
 204 |         self.order = order
 205 | 
 206 |     @staticmethod
 207 |     def _combinations(
 208 |         n_features, min_degree, max_degree, interaction_only, include_bias
 209 |     ):
 210 |         comb = combinations if interaction_only else combinations_w_r
 211 |         start = max(1, min_degree)
 212 |         iter = chain.from_iterable(
 213 |             comb(range(n_features), i) for i in range(start, max_degree + 1)
 214 |         )
 215 |         if include_bias:
 216 |             iter = chain(comb(range(n_features), 0), iter)
 217 |         return iter
 218 | 
 219 |     @staticmethod
 220 |     def _num_combinations(
 221 |         n_features, min_degree, max_degree, interaction_only, include_bias
 222 |     ):
 223 |         """Calculate number of terms in polynomial expansion
 224 | 
 225 |         This should be equivalent to counting the number of terms returned by
 226 |         _combinations(...) but much faster.
 227 |         """
 228 | 
 229 |         if interaction_only:
 230 |             combinations = sum(
 231 |                 [
 232 |                     comb(n_features, i, exact=True)
 233 |                     for i in range(max(1, min_degree), min(max_degree, n_features) + 1)
 234 |                 ]
 235 |             )
 236 |         else:
 237 |             combinations = comb(n_features + max_degree, max_degree, exact=True) - 1
 238 |             if min_degree > 0:
 239 |                 d = min_degree - 1
 240 |                 combinations -= comb(n_features + d, d, exact=True) - 1
 241 | 
 242 |         if include_bias:
 243 |             combinations += 1
 244 | 
 245 |         return combinations
 246 | 
 247 |     @property
 248 |     def powers_(self):
 249 |         """Exponent for each of the inputs in the output."""
 250 |         check_is_fitted(self)
 251 | 
 252 |         combinations = self._combinations(
 253 |             n_features=self.n_features_in_,
 254 |             min_degree=self._min_degree,
 255 |             max_degree=self._max_degree,
 256 |             interaction_only=self.interaction_only,
 257 |             include_bias=self.include_bias,
 258 |         )
 259 |         return np.vstack(
 260 |             [np.bincount(c, minlength=self.n_features_in_) for c in combinations]
 261 |         )
 262 | 
 263 |     def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
 264 |         """Get output feature names for transformation.
 265 | 
 266 |         Parameters
 267 |         ----------
 268 |         input_features : array-like of str or None, default=None
 269 |             Input features.
 270 | 
 271 |             - If `input_features is None`, then `feature_names_in_` is
 272 |               used as feature names in. If `feature_names_in_` is not defined,
 273 |               then the following input feature names are generated:
 274 |               `["x0", "x1", ..., "x(n_features_in_ - 1)"]`.
 275 |             - If `input_features` is an array-like, then `input_features` must
 276 |               match `feature_names_in_` if `feature_names_in_` is defined.
 277 | 
 278 |         Returns
 279 |         -------
 280 |         feature_names_out : ndarray of str objects
 281 |             Transformed feature names.
 282 |         """
 283 |         powers = self.powers_
 284 |         input_features = _check_feature_names_in(self, input_features)
 285 |         feature_names = []
 286 |         for row in powers:
 287 |             inds = np.where(row)[0]
 288 |             if len(inds):
 289 |                 name = " ".join(
 290 |                     (
 291 |                         "%s^%d" % (input_features[ind], exp)
 292 |                         if exp != 1
 293 |                         else input_features[ind]
 294 |                     )
 295 |                     for ind, exp in zip(inds, row[inds])
 296 |                 )
 297 |             else:
 298 |                 name = "1"
 299 |             feature_names.append(name)
 300 |         return np.asarray(feature_names, dtype=object)
 301 | 
 302 |     def fit(self, X, y=None):
 303 |         """
 304 |         Compute number of output features.
 305 | 
 306 |         Parameters
 307 |         ----------
 308 |         X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
 309 |             The data.
 310 | 
 311 |         y : Ignored
 312 |             Not used, present here for API consistency by convention.
 313 | 
 314 |         Returns
 315 |         -------
 316 |         self : object
 317 |             Fitted transformer.
 318 |         """
 319 |         self._validate_params()
 320 |         _, n_features = self._validate_data(X, accept_sparse=True).shape
 321 | 
 322 |         if isinstance(self.degree, Integral):
 323 |             if self.degree == 0 and not self.include_bias:
 324 |                 raise ValueError(
 325 |                     "Setting degree to zero and include_bias to False would result in"
 326 |                     " an empty output array."
 327 |                 )
 328 | 
 329 |             self._min_degree = 0
 330 |             self._max_degree = self.degree
 331 |         elif (
 332 |             isinstance(self.degree, collections.abc.Iterable) and len(self.degree) == 2
 333 |         ):
 334 |             self._min_degree, self._max_degree = self.degree
 335 |             if not (
 336 |                 isinstance(self._min_degree, Integral)
 337 |                 and isinstance(self._max_degree, Integral)
 338 |                 and self._min_degree >= 0
 339 |                 and self._min_degree <= self._max_degree
 340 |             ):
 341 |                 raise ValueError(
 342 |                     "degree=(min_degree, max_degree) must "
 343 |                     "be non-negative integers that fulfil "
 344 |                     "min_degree <= max_degree, got "
 345 |                     f"{self.degree}."
 346 |                 )
 347 |             elif self._max_degree == 0 and not self.include_bias:
 348 |                 raise ValueError(
 349 |                     "Setting both min_degree and max_degree to zero and include_bias to"
 350 |                     " False would result in an empty output array."
 351 |                 )
 352 |         else:
 353 |             raise ValueError(
 354 |                 "degree must be a non-negative int or tuple "
 355 |                 "(min_degree, max_degree), got "
 356 |                 f"{self.degree}."
 357 |             )
 358 | 
 359 |         self.n_output_features_ = self._num_combinations(
 360 |             n_features=n_features,
 361 |             min_degree=self._min_degree,
 362 |             max_degree=self._max_degree,
 363 |             interaction_only=self.interaction_only,
 364 |             include_bias=self.include_bias,
 365 |         )
 366 |         if self.n_output_features_ > np.iinfo(np.intp).max:
 367 |             msg = (
 368 |                 "The output that would result from the current configuration would"
 369 |                 f" have {self.n_output_features_} features which is too large to be"
 370 |                 f" indexed by {np.intp().dtype.name}. Please change some or all of the"
 371 |                 " following:\n- The number of features in the input, currently"
 372 |                 f" {n_features=}\n- The range of degrees to calculate, currently"
 373 |                 f" [{self._min_degree}, {self._max_degree}]\n- Whether to include only"
 374 |                 f" interaction terms, currently {self.interaction_only}\n- Whether to"
 375 |                 f" include a bias term, currently {self.include_bias}."
 376 |             )
 377 |             if (
 378 |                 np.intp == np.int32
 379 |                 and self.n_output_features_ <= np.iinfo(np.int64).max
 380 |             ):  # pragma: nocover
 381 |                 msg += (
 382 |                     "\nNote that the current Python runtime has a limited 32 bit "
 383 |                     "address space and that this configuration would have been "
 384 |                     "admissible if run on a 64 bit Python runtime."
 385 |                 )
 386 |             raise ValueError(msg)
 387 |         # We also record the number of output features for
 388 |         # _max_degree = 0
 389 |         self._n_out_full = self._num_combinations(
 390 |             n_features=n_features,
 391 |             min_degree=0,
 392 |             max_degree=self._max_degree,
 393 |             interaction_only=self.interaction_only,
 394 |             include_bias=self.include_bias,
 395 |         )
 396 | 
 397 |         return self

 399 |     def transform(self, X):
 400 |         """Transform data to polynomial features.
 401 | 
 402 |         Parameters
 403 |         ----------
 404 |         X : {array-like, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, n_features)
 405 |             The data to transform, row by row.
 406 | 
 407 |             Prefer CSR over CSC for sparse input (for speed), but CSC is
 408 |             required if the degree is 4 or higher. If the degree is less than
 409 |             4 and the input format is CSC, it will be converted to CSR, have
 410 |             its polynomial features generated, then converted back to CSC.
 411 | 
 412 |             If the degree is 2 or 3, the method described in "Leveraging
 413 |             Sparsity to Speed Up Polynomial Feature Expansions of CSR Matrices
 414 |             Using K-Simplex Numbers" by Andrew Nystrom and John Hughes is
 415 |             used, which is much faster than the method used on CSC input. For
 416 |             this reason, a CSC input will be converted to CSR, and the output
 417 |             will be converted back to CSC prior to being returned, hence the
 418 |             preference of CSR.
 419 | 
 420 |         Returns
 421 |         -------
 422 |         XP : {ndarray, sparse matrix} of shape (n_samples, NP)
 423 |             The matrix of features, where `NP` is the number of polynomial
 424 |             features generated from the combination of inputs. If a sparse
 425 |             matrix is provided, it will be converted into a sparse
 426 |             `csr_matrix`.
 427 |         """
 428 |         check_is_fitted(self)
 429 | 
 430 |         X = self._validate_data(
 431 |             X, order="F", dtype=FLOAT_DTYPES, reset=False, accept_sparse=("csr", "csc")
 432 |         )
 433 | 
 434 |         n_samples, n_features = X.shape
 435 |         max_int32 = np.iinfo(np.int32).max
 436 |         if sparse.isspmatrix_csr(X):
 437 |             if self._max_degree > 3:
 438 |                 return self.transform(X.tocsc()).tocsr()
 439 |             to_stack = []
 440 |             if self.include_bias:
 441 |                 to_stack.append(
 442 |                     sparse.csr_matrix(np.ones(shape=(n_samples, 1), dtype=X.dtype))
 443 |                 )
 444 |             if self._min_degree <= 1 and self._max_degree > 0:
 445 |                 to_stack.append(X)
 446 | 
 447 |             cumulative_size = sum(mat.shape[1] for mat in to_stack)
 448 |             for deg in range(max(2, self._min_degree), self._max_degree + 1):
 449 |                 expanded = _create_expansion(
 450 |                     X=X,
 451 |                     interaction_only=self.interaction_only,
 452 |                     deg=deg,
 453 |                     n_features=n_features,
 454 |                     cumulative_size=cumulative_size,
 455 |                 )
 456 |                 if expanded is not None:
 457 |                     to_stack.append(expanded)
 458 |                     cumulative_size += expanded.shape[1]
 459 |             if len(to_stack) == 0:
 460 |                 # edge case: deal with empty matrix
 461 |                 XP = sparse.csr_matrix((n_samples, 0), dtype=X.dtype)
 462 |             else:
 463 |                 # `scipy.sparse.hstack` breaks in scipy<1.9.2
 464 |                 # when `n_output_features_ > max_int32`
 465 |                 all_int32 = all(mat.indices.dtype == np.int32 for mat in to_stack)
 466 |                 if (
 467 |                     sp_version < parse_version("1.9.2")
 468 |                     and self.n_output_features_ > max_int32
 469 |                     and all_int32
 470 |                 ):
 471 |                     raise ValueError(  # pragma: no cover
 472 |                         "In scipy versions `<1.9.2`, the function `scipy.sparse.hstack`"
 473 |                         " produces negative columns when:\n1. The output shape contains"
 474 |                         " `n_cols` too large to be represented by a 32bit signed"
 475 |                         " integer.\n2. All sub-matrices to be stacked have indices of"
 476 |                         " dtype `np.int32`.\nTo avoid this error, either use a version"
 477 |                         " of scipy `>=1.9.2` or alter the `PolynomialFeatures`"
 478 |                         " transformer to produce fewer than 2^31 output features"
 479 |                     )
 480 |                 XP = sparse.hstack(to_stack, dtype=X.dtype, format="csr")
 481 |         elif sparse.isspmatrix_csc(X) and self._max_degree < 4:
 482 |             return self.transform(X.tocsr()).tocsc()
 483 |         elif sparse.isspmatrix(X):
 484 |             combinations = self._combinations(
 485 |                 n_features=n_features,
 486 |                 min_degree=self._min_degree,
 487 |                 max_degree=self._max_degree,
 488 |                 interaction_only=self.interaction_only,
 489 |                 include_bias=self.include_bias,
 490 |             )
 491 |             columns = []
 492 |             for combi in combinations:
 493 |                 if combi:
 494 |                     out_col = 1
 495 |                     for col_idx in combi:
 496 |                         out_col = X[:, col_idx].multiply(out_col)
 497 |                     columns.append(out_col)
 498 |                 else:
 499 |                     bias = sparse.csc_matrix(np.ones((X.shape[0], 1)))
 500 |                     columns.append(bias)
 501 |             XP = sparse.hstack(columns, dtype=X.dtype).tocsc()
 502 |         else:
 503 |             # Do as if _min_degree = 0 and cut down array after the
 504 |             # computation, i.e. use _n_out_full instead of n_output_features_.
 505 |             XP = np.empty(
 506 |                 shape=(n_samples, self._n_out_full), dtype=X.dtype, order=self.order
 507 |             )
 508 | 
 509 |             # What follows is a faster implementation of:
 510 |             # for i, comb in enumerate(combinations):
 511 |             #     XP[:, i] = X[:, comb].prod(1)
 512 |             # This implementation uses two optimisations.
 513 |             # First one is broadcasting,
 514 |             # multiply ([X1, ..., Xn], X1) -> [X1 X1, ..., Xn X1]
 515 |             # multiply ([X2, ..., Xn], X2) -> [X2 X2, ..., Xn X2]
 516 |             # ...
 517 |             # multiply ([X[:, start:end], X[:, start]) -> ...
 518 |             # Second optimisation happens for degrees >= 3.
 519 |             # Xi^3 is computed reusing previous computation:
 520 |             # Xi^3 = Xi^2 * Xi.
 521 | 
 522 |             # degree 0 term
 523 |             if self.include_bias:
 524 |                 XP[:, 0] = 1
 525 |                 current_col = 1
 526 |             else:
 527 |                 current_col = 0
 528 | 
 529 |             if self._max_degree == 0:
 530 |                 return XP
 531 | 
 532 |             # degree 1 term
 533 |             XP[:, current_col : current_col + n_features] = X
 534 |             index = list(range(current_col, current_col + n_features))
 535 |             current_col += n_features
 536 |             index.append(current_col)
 537 | 
 538 |             # loop over degree >= 2 terms
 539 |             for _ in range(2, self._max_degree + 1):
 540 |                 new_index = []
 541 |                 end = index[-1]
 542 |                 for feature_idx in range(n_features):
 543 |                     start = index[feature_idx]
 544 |                     new_index.append(current_col)
 545 |                     if self.interaction_only:
 546 |                         start += index[feature_idx + 1] - index[feature_idx]
 547 |                     next_col = current_col + end - start
 548 |                     if next_col <= current_col:
 549 |                         break
 550 |                     # XP[:, start:end] are terms of degree d - 1
 551 |                     # that exclude feature #feature_idx.
 552 |                     np.multiply(
 553 |                         XP[:, start:end],
 554 |                         X[:, feature_idx : feature_idx + 1],
 555 |                         out=XP[:, current_col:next_col],
 556 |                         casting="no",
 557 |                     )
 558 |                     current_col = next_col
 559 | 
 560 |                 new_index.append(current_col)
 561 |                 index = new_index
 562 | 
 563 |             if self._min_degree > 1:
 564 |                 n_XP, n_Xout = self._n_out_full, self.n_output_features_
 565 |                 if self.include_bias:
 566 |                     Xout = np.empty(
 567 |                         shape=(n_samples, n_Xout), dtype=XP.dtype, order=self.order
 568 |                     )
 569 |                     Xout[:, 0] = 1
 570 |                     Xout[:, 1:] = XP[:, n_XP - n_Xout + 1 :]
 571 |                 else:
 572 |                     Xout = XP[:, n_XP - n_Xout :].copy()
 573 |                 XP = Xout
 574 |         return XP

 579 | class SplineTransformer(TransformerMixin, BaseEstimator):
 580 |     """Generate univariate B-spline bases for features.
 581 | 
 582 |     Generate a new feature matrix consisting of
 583 |     `n_splines=n_knots + degree - 1` (`n_knots - 1` for
 584 |     `extrapolation="periodic"`) spline basis functions
 585 |     (B-splines) of polynomial order=`degree` for each feature.
 586 | 
 587 |     Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <spline_transformer>`.
 588 | 
 589 |     .. versionadded:: 1.0
 590 | 
 591 |     Parameters
 592 |     ----------
 593 |     n_knots : int, default=5
 594 |         Number of knots of the splines if `knots` equals one of
 595 |         {'uniform', 'quantile'}. Must be larger or equal 2. Ignored if `knots`
 596 |         is array-like.
 597 | 
 598 |     degree : int, default=3
 599 |         The polynomial degree of the spline basis. Must be a non-negative
 600 |         integer.
 601 | 
 602 |     knots : {'uniform', 'quantile'} or array-like of shape \
 603 |         (n_knots, n_features), default='uniform'
 604 |         Set knot positions such that first knot <= features <= last knot.
 605 | 
 606 |         - If 'uniform', `n_knots` number of knots are distributed uniformly
 607 |           from min to max values of the features.
 608 |         - If 'quantile', they are distributed uniformly along the quantiles of
 609 |           the features.
 610 |         - If an array-like is given, it directly specifies the sorted knot
 611 |           positions including the boundary knots. Note that, internally,
 612 |           `degree` number of knots are added before the first knot, the same
 613 |           after the last knot.
 614 | 
 615 |     extrapolation : {'error', 'constant', 'linear', 'continue', 'periodic'}, \
 616 |         default='constant'
 617 |         If 'error', values outside the min and max values of the training
 618 |         features raises a `ValueError`. If 'constant', the value of the
 619 |         splines at minimum and maximum value of the features is used as
 620 |         constant extrapolation. If 'linear', a linear extrapolation is used.
 621 |         If 'continue', the splines are extrapolated as is, i.e. option
 622 |         `extrapolate=True` in :class:`scipy.interpolate.BSpline`. If
 623 |         'periodic', periodic splines with a periodicity equal to the distance
 624 |         between the first and last knot are used. Periodic splines enforce
 625 |         equal function values and derivatives at the first and last knot.
 626 |         For example, this makes it possible to avoid introducing an arbitrary
 627 |         jump between Dec 31st and Jan 1st in spline features derived from a
 628 |         naturally periodic "day-of-year" input feature. In this case it is
 629 |         recommended to manually set the knot values to control the period.
 630 | 
 631 |     include_bias : bool, default=True
 632 |         If False, then the last spline element inside the data range
 633 |         of a feature is dropped. As B-splines sum to one over the spline basis
 634 |         functions for each data point, they implicitly include a bias term,
 635 |         i.e. a column of ones. It acts as an intercept term in a linear models.
 636 | 
 637 |     order : {'C', 'F'}, default='C'
 638 |         Order of output array. 'F' order is faster to compute, but may slow
 639 |         down subsequent estimators.
 640 | 
 641 |     Attributes
 642 |     ----------
 643 |     bsplines_ : list of shape (n_features,)
 644 |         List of BSplines objects, one for each feature.

** Note:
- Either `search_terms` or `line_nums` must be provided to perform a search.

- If `line_nums` is provided, it searches for code snippets around the specified lines within the file defined by `file_path_or_pattern`.

** Example Usage:
# Search for code content contain keyword `order`, `bill`
search_code_snippets(search_terms=["order", "bill"])

# Search for a class
search_code_snippets(search_terms=["MyClass"])

# Search for context around specific lines (10 and 15) within a file
search_code_snippets(line_nums=[10, 15], file_path_or_pattern='src/example.py')

search_terms.description: A list of names, keywords, or code snippets to search for within the codebase. This can include potential function names, class names, or general code fragments. Either `search_terms` or `line_nums` must be provided to perform a search.

line_nums.description: Specific line numbers to locate code snippets within a specified file. Must be used alongside a valid `file_path_or_pattern`. Either `line_nums` or `search_terms` must be provided to perform a search.

file_path_or_pattern.description: A glob pattern or specific file path used to filter search results to particular files or directories. Defaults to "**/*.py", meaning all Python files are searched by default. If `line_nums` are provided, this must specify a specific file path.

        4  foo  two  small  3  6

        6  bar  one  small  5  8
        7  bar  two  small  6  9
        8  bar  two  large  7  9

search_code_snippets(search_terms: Optional[List[str]] = None, line_nums: Optional[List] = None, file_path_or_pattern: Optional[str] = '**/*.py') -> str:
    Searches the codebase to retrieve relevant code snippets based on given queries(terms or line numbers).
    This function supports retrieving the complete content of a code entity,
    searching for code entities such as classes or functions by keywords, or locating specific lines within a file.
    It also supports filtering searches based on a file path or file pattern.
    Note:
    1. If `search_terms` are provided, it searches for code snippets based on each term:
    - If a term is formatted as 'file_path:QualifiedName' (e.g., 'src/helpers/math_helpers.py:MathUtils.calculate_sum') ,
    or just 'file_path', the corresponding complete code is retrieved or file content is retrieved.
    - If a term matches a file, class, or function name, matched entities are retrieved.
    - If there is no match with any module name, it attempts to find code snippets that likely contain the term.
    2. If `line_nums` is provided, it searches for code snippets at the specified lines within the file defined by
    `file_path_or_pattern`.
    Args:
    search_terms (Optional[List[str]]): A list of names, keywords, or code snippets to search for within the codebase.
    Terms can be formatted as 'file_path:QualifiedName' to search for a specific module or entity within a file
    (e.g., 'src/helpers/math_helpers.py:MathUtils.calculate_sum') or as 'file_path' to retrieve the complete content
    of a file. This can also include potential function names, class names, or general code fragments.
    line_nums (Optional[List[int]]): Specific line numbers to locate code snippets within a specified file.
    When provided, `file_path_or_pattern` must specify a valid file path.
    file_path_or_pattern (Optional[str]): A glob pattern or specific file path used to filter search results
    to particular files or directories. Defaults to '**/*.py', meaning all Python files are searched by default.
    If `line_nums` are provided, this must specify a specific file path.
    Returns:
    str: The search results, which may include code snippets, matching entities, or complete file content.
    Example Usage:
    # Search for the full content of a specific file
    result = search_code_snippets(search_terms=['src/my_file.py'])
    # Search for a specific function
    result = search_code_snippets(search_terms=['src/my_file.py:MyClass.func_name'])
    # Search for specific lines (10 and 15) within a file
    result = search_code_snippets(line_nums=[10, 15], file_path_or_pattern='src/example.py')
    # Combined search for a module name and within a specific file pattern
    result = search_code_snippets(search_terms=["MyClass"], file_path_or_pattern="src/**/*.py")

Searches the codebase to retrieve relevant code snippets based on given queries(terms or line numbers).
** Note:
- Either `search_terms` or `line_nums` must be provided to perform a search.
- If `search_terms` are provided, it searches for code snippets based on each term:
- If `line_nums` is provided, it searches for code snippets around the specified lines within the file defined by `file_path_or_pattern`.

** Example Usage:
# Search for code content contain keyword `order`, `bill`
search_code_snippets(search_terms=["order", "bill"])

# Search for a class
search_code_snippets(search_terms=["MyClass"])

# Search for context around specific lines (10 and 15) within a file
search_code_snippets(line_nums=[10, 15], file_path_or_pattern='src/example.py')

search_terms.description: A list of names, keywords, or code snippets to search for within the codebase. This can include potential function names, class names, or general code fragments. Either `search_terms` or `line_nums` must be provided to perform a search.

line_nums.description: Specific line numbers to locate code snippets within a specified file. Must be used alongside a valid `file_path_or_pattern`. Either `line_nums` or `search_terms` must be provided to perform a search.

file_path_or_pattern.description: A glob pattern or specific file path used to filter search results to particular files or directories. Defaults to "**/*.py", meaning all Python files are searched by default. If `line_nums` are provided, this must specify a specific file path.

Searches the codebase to retrieve the complete implementations of specified entities based on the provided entity names. 
The tool can handle specific entity queries such as function names, class names, or file paths.

**Usage Example:**
# Search for a specific function implementation
get_entity_contents(['src/my_file.py:MyClass.func_name'])

meta_data.problem_statement:
MAINT conversion old->new/new->old tags
Towards #30298 

This PR provides a way to convert old tags into new tags and new tags into old tags.
We should make sure that:

- An estimator implementing `_get_tags` or `_more_tags` get a warning but that the check_estimator should be working reasonably
- `_safe_tags` should raise a deprecation warning
- we should make sure that `get_tags` can get old tags and convert it to new tags. The tricky part is to detect whether `__sklearn_tags__` if present is implemented by the `BaseEstimator` from scikit-learn or the child class. If this is only the `BaseEstimator`, we should raise a warning to move to the new API and we should temporary use the `_get_tags`/`_safe_tags`, otherwise we are fine.

meta_data.problem_statement:
Reduce redundancy in floating type checks for Array API support
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

While working on #29978, we noticed that the following procedure is repeated across most regression metrics in `_regression.py` for the Array API:

```python
    xp, _ = get_namespace(y_true, y_pred, sample_weight, multioutput)
    dtype = _find_matching_floating_dtype(y_true, y_pred, xp=xp)

    _, y_true, y_pred, multioutput = _check_reg_targets(
        y_true, y_pred, multioutput, dtype=dtype, xp=xp
    )
```

To reduce redundancy, it would make sense to incorporate the `_find_matching_floating_dtype` logic directly into the `_check_reg_targets` function. This would result in the following cleaner implementation:

```python
    xp, _ = get_namespace(y_true, y_pred, sample_weight, multioutput)
    _, y_true, y_pred, multioutput, dtype = _check_reg_targets(
        y_true, y_pred, multioutput, xp=xp
    )
```

### Describe your proposed solution

We could introduce a new function, `_check_reg_targets_and_dtype`, defined in the obvious way. This approach would enable us to utilise the existing tests in `test_regression.py` with minimal changes.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

We could modify the original `_check_reg_targets` function, but this would require carefully reviewing and updating the relevant tests in `test_regression.py` to ensure everything remains consistent.

### Additional context

This is part of the Array API project #26024.

Title: Reduce redundancy in floating type checks for Array API support

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

While working on #29978, we noticed that the following procedure is repeated across most regression metrics in `_regression.py` for the Array API:

```python
    xp, _ = get_namespace(y_true, y_pred, sample_weight, multioutput)
    dtype = _find_matching_floating_dtype(y_true, y_pred, xp=xp)

    _, y_true, y_pred, multioutput = _check_reg_targets(
        y_true, y_pred, multioutput, dtype=dtype, xp=xp
    )
```

To reduce redundancy, it would make sense to incorporate the `_find_matching_floating_dtype` logic directly into the `_check_reg_targets` function. This would result in the following cleaner implementation:

```python
    xp, _ = get_namespace(y_true, y_pred, sample_weight, multioutput)
    _, y_true, y_pred, multioutput, dtype = _check_reg_targets(
        y_true, y_pred, multioutput, xp=xp
    )
```

### Describe your proposed solution

We could introduce a new function, `_check_reg_targets_and_dtype`, defined in the obvious way. This approach would enable us to utilise the existing tests in `test_regression.py` with minimal changes.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

We could modify the original `_check_reg_targets` function, but this would require carefully reviewing and updating the relevant tests in `test_regression.py` to ensure everything remains consistent.

 347 |     if type_.__module__ == "builtins":
 348 |         type_name = type_.__qualname__
 349 |     else:
 350 |         type_name = f"{type_.__module__}.{type_.__qualname__}"
 351 |     message = f"Unable to find the number of features from X of type {type_name}"
 352 |     if not hasattr(X, "__len__") and not hasattr(X, "shape"):
 353 |         if not hasattr(X, "__array__"):
 354 |             raise TypeError(message)
 355 |         # Only convert X to a numpy array if there is no cheaper, heuristic
 356 |         # option.
 357 |         X = np.asarray(X)
 358 | 
 359 |     if hasattr(X, "shape"):
 360 |         if not hasattr(X.shape, "__len__") or len(X.shape) <= 1:
 361 |             message += f" with shape {X.shape}"
 362 |             raise TypeError(message)
 363 |         return X.shape[1]
 364 | 
 365 |     first_sample = X[0]
 366 | 
 367 |     # Do not consider an array-like of strings or dicts to be a 2D array
 368 |     if isinstance(first_sample, (str, bytes, dict)):
 369 |         message += f" where the samples are of type {type(first_sample).__qualname__}"
 370 |         raise TypeError(message)
 371 | 
 372 |     try:
 373 |         # If X is a list of lists, for instance, we assume that all nested
 374 |         # lists have the same length without checking or converting to
 375 |         # a numpy array to keep this function call as cheap as possible.
 376 |         return len(first_sample)
 377 |     except Exception as err:
 378 |         raise TypeError(message) from err

 381 | def _num_samples(x):
 382 |     """Return number of samples in array-like x."""
 383 |     message = "Expected sequence or array-like, got %s" % type(x)
 384 |     if hasattr(x, "fit") and callable(x.fit):
 385 |         # Don't get num_samples from an ensembles length!
 386 |         raise TypeError(message)
 387 | 
 388 |     if _use_interchange_protocol(x):
 389 |         return x.__dataframe__().num_rows()
 390 | 
 391 |     if not hasattr(x, "__len__") and not hasattr(x, "shape"):
 392 |         if hasattr(x, "__array__"):
 393 |             x = np.asarray(x)
 394 |         else:
 395 |             raise TypeError(message)
 396 | 
 397 |     if hasattr(x, "shape") and x.shape is not None:
 398 |         if len(x.shape) == 0:
 399 |             raise TypeError(
 400 |                 "Singleton array %r cannot be considered a valid collection." % x
 401 |             )
 402 |         # Check that shape is returning an integer or default to len
 403 |         # Dask dataframes may not return numeric shape[0] value
 404 |         if isinstance(x.shape[0], numbers.Integral):
 405 |             return x.shape[0]
 406 | 
 407 |     try:
 408 |         return len(x)
 409 |     except TypeError as type_error:
 410 |         raise TypeError(message) from type_error

 480 | def _make_indexable(iterable):
 481 |     """Ensure iterable supports indexing or convert to an indexable variant.
 482 | 
 483 |     Convert sparse matrices to csr and other non-indexable iterable to arrays.
 484 |     Let `None` and indexable objects (e.g. pandas dataframes) pass unchanged.
 485 | 
 486 |     Parameters
 487 |     ----------
 488 |     iterable : {list, dataframe, ndarray, sparse matrix} or None
 489 |         Object to be converted to an indexable iterable.
 490 |     """
 491 |     if sp.issparse(iterable):
 492 |         return iterable.tocsr()
 493 |     elif hasattr(iterable, "__getitem__") or hasattr(iterable, "iloc"):
 494 |         return iterable
 495 |     elif iterable is None:
 496 |         return iterable

 502 | 
 503 |     Checks consistent length, passes through None, and ensures that everything
 504 |     can be indexed by converting sparse matrices to csr and converting
 505 |     non-iterable objects to arrays.

 507 |     Parameters
 508 |     ----------

 510 |         List of objects to ensure sliceability.

 513 |     -------
 514 |     result : list of {ndarray, sparse matrix, dataframe} or None
 515 |         Returns a list containing indexable arrays (i.e. NumPy array,
 516 |         sparse matrix, or dataframe) or `None`.
 517 |

 519 |     --------
 520 |     >>> from sklearn.utils import indexable
 521 |     >>> from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
 522 |     >>> import numpy as np

 524 |     ...     [1, 2, 3], np.array([2, 3, 4]), None, csr_matrix([[5], [6], [7]])
 525 |     ... ]

 535 | def _ensure_sparse_format(
 536 |     sparse_container,
 537 |     accept_sparse,
 538 |     dtype,
 539 |     copy,
 540 |     ensure_all_finite,
 541 |     accept_large_sparse,
 542 |     estimator_name=None,
 543 |     input_name="",
 544 | ):
 545 |     """Convert a sparse container to a given format.
 546 | 
 547 |     Checks the sparse format of `sparse_container` and converts if necessary.
 548 | 
 549 |     Parameters
 550 |     ----------
 551 |     sparse_container : sparse matrix or array
 552 |         Input to validate and convert.
 553 | 
 554 |     accept_sparse : str, bool or list/tuple of str
 555 |         String[s] representing allowed sparse matrix formats ('csc',
 556 |         'csr', 'coo', 'dok', 'bsr', 'lil', 'dia'). If the input is sparse but
 557 |         not in the allowed format, it will be converted to the first listed
 558 |         format. True allows the input to be any format. False means
 559 |         that a sparse matrix input will raise an error.
 560 | 
 561 |     dtype : str, type or None
 562 |         Data type of result. If None, the dtype of the input is preserved.
 563 | 
 564 |     copy : bool
 565 |         Whether a forced copy will be triggered. If copy=False, a copy might
 566 |         be triggered by a conversion.
 567 | 
 568 |     ensure_all_finite : bool or 'allow-nan'
 569 |         Whether to raise an error on np.inf, np.nan, pd.NA in X. The
 570 |         possibilities are:
 571 | 
 572 |         - True: Force all values of X to be finite.
 573 |         - False: accepts np.inf, np.nan, pd.NA in X.
 574 |         - 'allow-nan': accepts only np.nan and pd.NA values in X. Values cannot
 575 |           be infinite.
 576 | 
 577 |         .. versionadded:: 0.20
 578 |            ``ensure_all_finite`` accepts the string ``'allow-nan'``.
 579 | 
 580 |         .. versionchanged:: 0.23
 581 |            Accepts `pd.NA` and converts it into `np.nan`
 582 | 
 583 | 
 584 |     estimator_name : str, default=None
 585 |         The estimator name, used to construct the error message.
 586 | 
 587 |     input_name : str, default=""
 588 |         The data name used to construct the error message. In particular
 589 |         if `input_name` is "X" and the data has NaN values and
 590 |         allow_nan is False, the error message will link to the imputer
 591 |         documentation.
 592 | 
 593 |     Returns
 594 |     -------
 595 |     sparse_container_converted : sparse matrix or array
 596 |         Sparse container (matrix/array) that is ensured to have an allowed type.
 597 |     """
 598 |     if dtype is None:
 599 |         dtype = sparse_container.dtype
 600 | 
 601 |     changed_format = False
 602 |     sparse_container_type_name = type(sparse_container).__name__
 603 | 
 604 |     if isinstance(accept_sparse, str):
 605 |         accept_sparse = [accept_sparse]
 606 | 
 607 |     # Indices dtype validation
 608 |     _check_large_sparse(sparse_container, accept_large_sparse)
 609 | 
 610 |     if accept_sparse is False:
 611 |         padded_input = " for " + input_name if input_name else ""
 612 |         raise TypeError(
 613 |             f"Sparse data was passed{padded_input}, but dense data is required. "
 614 |             "Use '.toarray()' to convert to a dense numpy array."
 615 |         )
 616 |     elif isinstance(accept_sparse, (list, tuple)):
 617 |         if len(accept_sparse) == 0:
 618 |             raise ValueError(
 619 |                 "When providing 'accept_sparse' as a tuple or list, it must contain at "
 620 |                 "least one string value."
 621 |             )
 622 |         # ensure correct sparse format
 623 |         if sparse_container.format not in accept_sparse:
 624 |             # create new with correct sparse
 625 |             sparse_container = sparse_container.asformat(accept_sparse[0])
 626 |             changed_format = True
 627 |     elif accept_sparse is not True:
 628 |         # any other type
 629 |         raise ValueError(
 630 |             "Parameter 'accept_sparse' should be a string, boolean or list of strings."
 631 |             f" You provided 'accept_sparse={accept_sparse}'."
 632 |         )
 633 | 
 634 |     if dtype != sparse_container.dtype:
 635 |         # convert dtype
 636 |         sparse_container = sparse_container.astype(dtype)
 637 |     elif copy and not changed_format:
 638 |         # force copy
 639 |         sparse_container = sparse_container.copy()
 640 | 
 641 |     if ensure_all_finite:
 642 |         if not hasattr(sparse_container, "data"):
 643 |             warnings.warn(
 644 |                 f"Can't check {sparse_container.format} sparse matrix for nan or inf.",
 645 |                 stacklevel=2,
 646 |             )
 647 |         else:
 648 |             _assert_all_finite(
 649 |                 sparse_container.data,
 650 |                 allow_nan=ensure_all_finite == "allow-nan",
 651 |                 estimator_name=estimator_name,
 652 |                 input_name=input_name,
 653 |             )
 654 | 
 655 |     # TODO: Remove when the minimum version of SciPy supported is 1.12
 656 |     # With SciPy sparse arrays, conversion from DIA format to COO, CSR, or BSR
 657 |     # triggers the use of `np.int64` indices even if the data is such that it could
 658 |     # be more efficiently represented with `np.int32` indices.
 659 |     # https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/19245 Since not all scikit-learn
 660 |     # algorithms support large indices, the following code downcasts to `np.int32`
 661 |     # indices when it's safe to do so.
 662 |     if changed_format:
 663 |         # accept_sparse is specified to a specific format and a conversion occurred
 664 |         requested_sparse_format = accept_sparse[0]
 665 |         _preserve_dia_indices_dtype(
 666 |             sparse_container, sparse_container_type_name, requested_sparse_format
 667 |         )
 668 | 
 669 |     return sparse_container

 691 | def _pandas_dtype_needs_early_conversion(pd_dtype):

 693 |     # Check these early for pandas versions without extension dtypes

 698 |         is_integer_dtype,

 713 |         return False

 717 |         # Only handle extension arrays for integer and floats
 718 |         return False
 719 |     elif is_float_dtype(pd_dtype):

 721 |         # first to map pd.NA to np.nan
 722 |         return True
 723 |     elif is_integer_dtype(pd_dtype):
 724 |         # XXX: Warn when converting from a high integer to a float
 725 |         return True
 726 | 
 727 |     return False

1546 | def check_symmetric(array, *, tol=1e-10, raise_warning=True, raise_exception=False):
1547 |     """Make sure that array is 2D, square and symmetric.
1548 | 
1549 |     If the array is not symmetric, then a symmetrized version is returned.
1550 |     Optionally, a warning or exception is raised if the matrix is not
1551 |     symmetric.
1552 | 
1553 |     Parameters
1554 |     ----------
1555 |     array : {ndarray, sparse matrix}
1556 |         Input object to check / convert. Must be two-dimensional and square,
1557 |         otherwise a ValueError will be raised.
1558 | 
1559 |     tol : float, default=1e-10
1560 |         Absolute tolerance for equivalence of arrays. Default = 1E-10.
1561 | 
1562 |     raise_warning : bool, default=True
1563 |         If True then raise a warning if conversion is required.
1564 | 
1565 |     raise_exception : bool, default=False
1566 |         If True then raise an exception if array is not symmetric.
1567 | 
1568 |     Returns
1569 |     -------
1570 |     array_sym : {ndarray, sparse matrix}
1571 |         Symmetrized version of the input array, i.e. the average of array
1572 |         and array.transpose(). If sparse, then duplicate entries are first
1573 |         summed and zeros are eliminated.
1574 | 
1575 |     Examples
1576 |     --------
1577 |     >>> import numpy as np
1578 |     >>> from sklearn.utils.validation import check_symmetric
1579 |     >>> symmetric_array = np.array([[0, 1, 2], [1, 0, 1], [2, 1, 0]])
1580 |     >>> check_symmetric(symmetric_array)
1581 |     array([[0, 1, 2],
1582 |            [1, 0, 1],
1583 |            [2, 1, 0]])
1584 |     >>> from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
1585 |     >>> sparse_symmetric_array = csr_matrix(symmetric_array)
1586 |     >>> check_symmetric(sparse_symmetric_array)
1587 |     <Compressed Sparse Row sparse matrix of dtype 'int64'
1588 |         with 6 stored elements and shape (3, 3)>
1589 |     """
1590 |     if (array.ndim != 2) or (array.shape[0] != array.shape[1]):
1591 |         raise ValueError(
1592 |             "array must be 2-dimensional and square. shape = {0}".format(array.shape)
1593 |         )
1594 | 
1595 |     if sp.issparse(array):
1596 |         diff = array - array.T
1597 |         # only csr, csc, and coo have `data` attribute
1598 |         if diff.format not in ["csr", "csc", "coo"]:
1599 |             diff = diff.tocsr()
1600 |         symmetric = np.all(abs(diff.data) < tol)
1601 |     else:
1602 |         symmetric = np.allclose(array, array.T, atol=tol)
1603 | 
1604 |     if not symmetric:
1605 |         if raise_exception:
1606 |             raise ValueError("Array must be symmetric")
1607 |         if raise_warning:
1608 |             warnings.warn(
1609 |                 (
1610 |                     "Array is not symmetric, and will be converted "
1611 |                     "to symmetric by average with its transpose."
1612 |                 ),
1613 |                 stacklevel=2,
1614 |             )
1615 |         if sp.issparse(array):
1616 |             conversion = "to" + array.format
1617 |             array = getattr(0.5 * (array + array.T), conversion)()
1618 |         else:
1619 |             array = 0.5 * (array + array.T)
1620 | 
1621 |     return array

1624 | def _is_fitted(estimator, attributes=None, all_or_any=all):
1625 |     """Determine if an estimator is fitted

1627 |     Parameters

1637 |         attribute that ends with a underscore and does not start with double

1652 | 
1653 |     if hasattr(estimator, "__sklearn_is_fitted__"):
1654 |         return estimator.__sklearn_is_fitted__()
1655 | 
1656 |     fitted_attrs = [

1662 | def check_is_fitted(estimator, attributes=None, *, msg=None, all_or_any=all):
1663 |     """Perform is_fitted validation for estimator.
1664 | 
1665 |     Checks if the estimator is fitted by verifying the presence of
1666 |     fitted attributes (ending with a trailing underscore) and otherwise
1667 |     raises a :class:`~sklearn.exceptions.NotFittedError` with the given message.
1668 | 
1669 |     If an estimator does not set any attributes with a trailing underscore, it
1670 |     can define a ``__sklearn_is_fitted__`` method returning a boolean to
1671 |     specify if the estimator is fitted or not. See
1672 |     :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_developing_estimators_sklearn_is_fitted.py`
1673 |     for an example on how to use the API.
1674 | 
1675 |     If no `attributes` are passed, this fuction will pass if an estimator is stateless.
1676 |     An estimator can indicate it's stateless by setting the `requires_fit` tag. See
1677 |     :ref:`estimator_tags` for more information. Note that the `requires_fit` tag
1678 |     is ignored if `attributes` are passed.
1679 | 
1680 |     Parameters
1681 |     ----------
1682 |     estimator : estimator instance
1683 |         Estimator instance for which the check is performed.
1684 | 
1685 |     attributes : str, list or tuple of str, default=None
1686 |         Attribute name(s) given as string or a list/tuple of strings
1687 |         Eg.: ``["coef_", "estimator_", ...], "coef_"``
1688 | 
1689 |         If `None`, `estimator` is considered fitted if there exist an
1690 |         attribute that ends with a underscore and does not start with double
1691 |         underscore.
1692 | 
1693 |     msg : str, default=None
1694 |         The default error message is, "This %(name)s instance is not fitted
1695 |         yet. Call 'fit' with appropriate arguments before using this
1696 |         estimator."
1697 | 
1698 |         For custom messages if "%(name)s" is present in the message string,
1699 |         it is substituted for the estimator name.
1700 | 
1701 |         Eg. : "Estimator, %(name)s, must be fitted before sparsifying".
1702 | 
1703 |     all_or_any : callable, {all, any}, default=all
1704 |         Specify whether all or any of the given attributes must exist.
1705 | 
1706 |     Raises
1707 |     ------
1708 |     TypeError
1709 |         If the estimator is a class or not an estimator instance
1710 | 
1711 |     NotFittedError
1712 |         If the attributes are not found.
1713 | 
1714 |     Examples
1715 |     --------
1716 |     >>> from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
1717 |     >>> from sklearn.utils.validation import check_is_fitted
1718 |     >>> from sklearn.exceptions import NotFittedError
1719 |     >>> lr = LogisticRegression()
1720 |     >>> try:
1721 |     ...     check_is_fitted(lr)
1722 |     ... except NotFittedError as exc:
1723 |     ...     print(f"Model is not fitted yet.")
1724 |     Model is not fitted yet.
1725 |     >>> lr.fit([[1, 2], [1, 3]], [1, 0])
1726 |     LogisticRegression()
1727 |     >>> check_is_fitted(lr)
1728 |     """
1729 |     if isclass(estimator):
1730 |         raise TypeError("{} is a class, not an instance.".format(estimator))
1731 |     if msg is None:
1732 |         msg = (
1733 |             "This %(name)s instance is not fitted yet. Call 'fit' with "
1734 |             "appropriate arguments before using this estimator."
1735 |         )
1736 | 
1737 |     if not hasattr(estimator, "fit"):
1738 |         raise TypeError("%s is not an estimator instance." % (estimator))
1739 | 
1740 |     tags = get_tags(estimator)
1741 | 
1742 |     if not tags.requires_fit and attributes is None:
1743 |         return
1744 | 
1745 |     if not _is_fitted(estimator, attributes, all_or_any):
1746 |         raise NotFittedError(msg % {"name": type(estimator).__name__})

1749 | def _estimator_has(attr, *, delegates=("estimator_", "estimator")):
1750 |     """Check if we can delegate a method to the underlying estimator.
1751 | 
1752 |     We check the `delegates` in the order they are passed. By default, we first check
1753 |     the fitted estimator if available, otherwise we check the unfitted estimator.
1754 | 
1755 |     Parameters
1756 |     ----------
1757 |     attr : str
1758 |         Name of the attribute the delegate might or might not have.
1759 | 
1760 |     delegates: tuple of str, default=("estimator_", "estimator")
1761 |         A tuple of sub-estimator(s) to check if we can delegate the `attr` method.
1762 | 
1763 |     Returns
1764 |     -------
1765 |     check : function
1766 |         Function to check if the delegate has the attribute.
1767 | 
1768 |     Raises
1769 |     ------
1770 |     ValueError
1771 |         Raised when none of the delegates are present in the object.
1772 |     """
1773 | 
1774 |     def check(self):
1775 |         for delegate in delegates:
1776 |             # In meta estimators with multiple sub estimators,
1777 |             # only the attribute of the first sub estimator is checked,
1778 |             # assuming uniformity across all sub estimators.
1779 |             if hasattr(self, delegate):
1780 |                 delegator = getattr(self, delegate)
1781 |                 if isinstance(delegator, Sequence):
1782 |                     return getattr(delegator[0], attr)
1783 |                 else:
1784 |                     return getattr(delegator, attr)
1785 | 
1786 |         raise ValueError(f"None of the delegates {delegates} are present in the class.")
1787 | 
1788 |     return check
